articles.title: Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
articles.summary: The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit.
articles.full_text:
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit By Anthony Zurcher North America correspondent 
- Published 19 November 2026 
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return. 
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers. 
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting. 
- 
Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting 
- Published 3 days ago 
- 
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls 
- Published 3 days ago 
In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success. 
That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president. 
Figure caption, 
Trump greets 'my friend' Putin ahead of meeting with Xi 
So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting. 
While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday. 
On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington. 
For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique , released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security". 
That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric. 
"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC. 
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
The visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss issues of global importance might offer the world some reassurance 
A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire. 
If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts. 
While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader. 
But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely to face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism. 
"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday. 
"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are." 
Illinois Republican Congressman Darin LaHood, who was re-elected with Trump's endorsement earlier this month, says the US should have discussions with both allies and adversaries abroad. But he adds that Putin is a "dictator" and "an international criminal". 
"I worry a little bit about the images of giving him a platform on a world stage as somehow equal to the United States," he tells BBC News. 
"We have to remember what Putin has done in Ukraine," LaHood says. "He invaded a sovereign, independent, democratically-elected country, and continues to engage in aggression there." 
Democrats, for their part, did not mince words. 
"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House. 
Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats. 
In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten. 
Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

articles.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
articles.summary: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts By Kelly Ng 
- Published 20 November 2026 
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing. 
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports. 
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday. 
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September. 
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on. 
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans. 
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time. 
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters". 
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others." 
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents. 
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails. 
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level. 
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight." 
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m. 
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather. 
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

articles.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
articles.summary: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit By Laura Bicker China correspondent ,  Reporting from Shenzhen 
- Published 19 November 2026 
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen. 
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order. 
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table. 
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets. 
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics. 
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order. 
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump. 
- 
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines 
Ukraine, the balancing act 
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda. 
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports. 
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour. 
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fifth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives 
The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas. 
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems. 
China's growing nuclear arsenal 
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons. 
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington. 
The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal. 
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back. 
Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025 
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power. 
Will everyone stick to the script? 
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish. 
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches. 
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders. 
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script. 
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment. 
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands. 
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end. 
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman. 
Xi's problems at home 
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes. 
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy 
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges. 
A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely. 
Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow. 
At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title: A new Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit
articles.summary: Trade, connectivity and regional cooperation will be on top of the agenda when Nepal's PM meets his India counterpart.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit By Anbarasan Ethirajan Global Affairs Correspondent 
- Published 20 November 2026 
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour. 
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government. 
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials. 
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August. 
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for. 
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles). 
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing 
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi. 
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset. 
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC. 
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds. 
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance. 
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them – the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN – UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre). 
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements. 
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal. 
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests. 
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily. 
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties 
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further. 
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae. 
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year. 
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences. 
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region. 
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas. 
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC. 
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination. 
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable. 
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance . 
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours. 
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus. 
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations. 
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough. 
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit. 
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office. 
Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom. 
While Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

articles.title: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
articles.summary: Lawyers will study the way in which The Gambia proved the crucial point that Myanmar intended to commit genocide, writes the BBC's international editor.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Rohingya refugees at a camp in Bangladesh cheered as the verdict was handed down by the president of the International Court of Justice By Jeremy Bowen International editor 
- Published 19 November 2026 
This judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention. 
The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017. 
In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict. 
He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since The Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes. 
- 
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules 
- Published 3 days ago 
The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent. 
They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation. 
The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
This was the first time an international court has found a state guilty of genocide 
The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences. 
Lawyers will study the way in which The Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide. 
Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough. 
The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group". 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
More than 700,000 Rohingya were forced to flee over the border to Bangladesh 
The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof. 
That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed. 
In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get. 
Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people. 
According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent. 
"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective." 
In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide. 
Figure caption, 
Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now? 
The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza. 
The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of The Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one". 
The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgment on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide. 
"If The Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over. 
"But The Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards." 
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade. 
The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas. 
That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court. 
The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity". 
It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days. 
Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both. 
Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people. 
But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide". 
Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ. 
He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case. 
She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: South East Asia correspondent Jonathan Head witnessed Rohingya villages burned down 
But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago. 
It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel. 
"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University. 
"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital By Tara Mewawalla 
- Published 21 November 2026 Updated 22 November 2026 
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities. 
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said. 
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added. 
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition. 
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House. 
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile. 
Image source, FBI Image caption, 
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday 
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said. 
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued. 
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds. 
Eight people in total were arrested, including Meza Flores' second-in-command, who is also his cousin, and his brother-in-law, who is the group's financial operator, the secretariat added. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Moment Mexican reporter takes cover on air as gunshots ring out nearby 
Meza Flores, his cousin, and his brother-in-law were flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said. The other five remained in the state of Sinaloa. 
Authorities also said they had seized multiple weapons during the operation, including a grenade launcher, as well as drugs and cash. 
The US Consulate General in the city of Hermosillo said it was "monitoring reports of ongoing security operations, armed clashes, road blockades, and vehicle fires that occurred overnight in Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave, and Navolato" following the arrest of Meza-Flores.  
It advised US citizens to remain alert for potential violence in the area and for residents to remain sheltered in place. 
When Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture. 
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico. 
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019. 
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was arrested 
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013. 
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region. 
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024. 
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground. 
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, 
Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine By Sarah Rainsford ,  Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent in Kyiv   and   Jaroslav Lukiv 
- Published 21 November 2026 
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine. 
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate". 
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use. 
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said. 
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics. 
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that." 
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine. 
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic. 
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time. 
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city. 
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west. 
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. 
Figure caption, 
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge 
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support. 
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said. 
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation". 
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence". 
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer". 
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend". 
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine. 
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic". 
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". 
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks". 
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. 
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war. 
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate." 
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions." 
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area". 
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details. 
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons. 
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
articles.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold? By Rachel Clun   and   Jemma Crew ,  Business reporters 
- Published 20 November 2026 
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. 
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. 
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. 
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. 
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago. 
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when. 
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development. 
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday. 
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17. 
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers. 
Image source, Getty Images 
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading. 
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market. 
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth. 
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said. 
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability." 
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued. 
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices. 
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record. 
But tech stocks more broadly also fell. 
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls. 
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit. 
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower. 
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls. 
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses. 
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
articles.summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship".
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend' By Jessica Lamb 
- Published 21 November 2026 
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week. 
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer". 
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years". 
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said. 
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west. 
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones. 
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge. 
Image source, EPA 
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war". 
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday. 
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US. 
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer". 
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN. 
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure". 
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday. 
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border. 
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added. 
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare". 
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe. 
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow. 
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response. 
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine. 
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips 
Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”. 
The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom. 
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees. Howard Lutnick has been Trump’s ally for decades. His ties to Nvidia may spell his downfall 
Read more 
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China. 
On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips. 
He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.” 
Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”. 
“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said. 
Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it. 
Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”. 
He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”. 
View image in fullscreen 
John Kennedy speaks to the media on 10 November, the day of the Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington DC. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters 
“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said. 
Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company. 
“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program. 
Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl. 
Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
District court in the Hague finds Chinese carmaker infringed on intellectual property of Jaguar Land Rover 
Chinese carmaker BYD has been banned from selling its “Defender clone” vehicle in the EU by a court in the Netherlands, after Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought a case saying it infringed intellectual property rights. 
JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices . 
“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that ​the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover ,” said the ruling from the district court in The Hague. “The characteristic ⁠and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.” 
View image in fullscreen 
A Land Rover Defender 110 on display at the 2019 Frankfurt Motor Show in Germany. Photograph: Ralph Orlowski/Reuters 
The ban will take effect one week after Friday’s ruling, which noted that BYD “currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU”. The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD’s activities in the UK. 
BYD’s plug-in hybrid SUV, which has been on sale in China since last September, has been likened by motoring experts to the Land Rover Defender, with the BBC’s Top Gear magazine calling it the “Chinese Defender clone” .

The Ti7 has gone on sale in the UK for £47,995, more than £20,000 cheaper than the Defender, with deliveries to customers due from January 2027. 
JLR’s seven-seat Defender is one of the UK’s bestselling cars and is the company’s most popular model. The UK-based carmaker, which is owned by India’s Tata Motors, sold 29,500 Defenders to retail customers between July and September this year, an increase of more than 4,000 on the same period a year earlier. 
JLR said in a statement: “We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary. Legal proceedings are ongoing and we won’t be commenting ​further at this time.” 
In ​a statement, BYD ⁠said it “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and will appeal. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” BYD said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision ⁠is incorrect.” 
The court also banned BYD from producing the vehicle at its new factory at Szeged in Hungary, which is expected to start producing cars at the end of 2026, until the intellectual property case is resolved. 
While many traditional carmakers have complained for some time that Chinese competitors have copied their designs, until now little has been tested in court. It is it relatively rare for European automakers to go to court over infringement of design rights. 
However, JLR previously won a legal case to stop Jiangling Motors Corporation selling a copycat vehicle in 2019, after a three-year court battle.
